record.title: RNED: Rotary Number Encoding and Decoding for Medical VLMs

datasets.name: Opport-CT
datasets.anchor:
We evaluate RNED on two tasks: quantitative radiology
estimation (on the in-house Opport-CT dataset and the public
CT-RATE [15]) and medical vision grounding (on the public
MedSeq-Bench [45]).
Opport-CT Dataset is a large-scale, in-house dataset com-
piled for an opportunistic screening study and consists of
25,645 non-contrast CT volumes, each paired with a ra-
diology report. Following methodologies from CT-RATE
and HuatuoGPT [9], we employed a two-pronged genera-
tion strategy to acquire diverse Visual Question Answering
(VQA) dataset for each volume-report pair. The overall gen-
eration process and samples are illustrated in Supp. Sec. 7.5.

datasets.name: CT-RATE
datasets.anchor:
CT-RATE Dataset is a public dataset containing over 50,000
image-report pairs from 21,304 patients, with CT images
acquired using various reconstruction techniques [15]. We
leverage the VQA data provided with the dataset, which
includes a mix of long-answer, short-answer, and multiple-
choice questions derived from the radiology reports.

datasets.name: MedSeq-Bench
datasets.anchor:
MedSeq-Bench Dataset is a public benchmark for eval-
uating medical VLM grounding [45], with 1,000 image-
question-answer triplets across 8 tasks in two categories: Im-
age Difference Grounding (IDG), which localizes changed
regions between temporally related images, and Image Con-
sistency Grounding (ICG), which localizes corresponding
regions across image pairs (e.g., multi-view matching, ob-
ject tracking, cross-modal alignment). Each task requires
bounding-box coordinate prediction, making it an ideal
testbed for RNED.

We use OneStop (Berzak et al., 2025a), a public eye tracking dataset collected with an EyeLink 1000
Plus eye tracker. It comprises 360 adult native English speakers reading Guardian articles from the
OneStopQA multiple choice reading comprehension dataset (Vajjala & Luˇci´c, 2018; Berzak et al.,
2020). In each experimental trial, a participant reads a paragraph on a screen and, on the following
screen, answers a multiple-choice reading comprehension question, without the ability to return to
the paragraph. Each paragraph can appear in its original or human-simplified form. 180 participants
read in an information seeking condition, where they receive the question (but not the answers)
before reading the paragraph, and therefore have a specific reading goal for the upcoming paragraph.
The remaining 180 participants do not receive the question ahead of time, and thus have to be ready
to answer any subsequent question. We use the information seeking part of OneStop (Berzak et al.,
2025b), which is uniquely suited for our study.
